Seagull Enterprises, Inc., renamed Seagull Inc. in 1977, was an American distributor of sports timing
equipment, based in California, that represented the timing division of Omega in the United States
and Canada through most of the 1970s.[^sw7309][^sw7706] It sold, rented and serviced the
[Swim-O-Matic](../equipment/swimming/timers/swim-o-matic.md), [OSM-3](../equipment/swimming/timers/osm-3.md),
[OSM-4](../equipment/swimming/timers/osm-4.md) and [OSM-5](../equipment/swimming/timers/osm-5.md) systems,
and later added stopwatches and training aids from other makers.[^sw7305][^sn46] Everything known
about the company comes from its advertising and from swimming magazines of the period.

## History

Seagull said in October 1974 that it had brought Omega timing to the United States and Canada two years
earlier, which places the start at about 1972.[^sw7410] The earliest advertisement found is from May
1973, when the company was at 2200 Sand Hill Road in Menlo Park.[^sw7305] Its advertisements carried the line "Exclusive United States and Canadian representative for Omega Electronic Division".[^sw7309]
Omega equipment had reached some North American pools before this: a customer quoted by Seagull in 1976
said the White Plains YWCA in New York had used Omega since 1971.[^sw7608] No source explains how those
pools obtained it, and no source names Seagull's founders or owners.

The company moved to 105 Main Street in Los Altos by December 1973, to 95 Main Street by March 1976, and
to 630 Cowper Street in Palo Alto by December 1976.[^sw7312][^sw7603][^sw7612] In 1976 it had an Omega
Timing Division and an American Aquatics Division, and its staff included Greg Fink as operations manager
and Doug Vaughn as marketing manager.[^sw7603][^sw7607] The name Seagull Inc. appears from June 1977, though
one advertisement of the following month keeps the earlier name.[^sw7706][^sw7707]

Seagull expanded in Canada in 1977. Mike Gibbons, an electronics engineer and Canadian Amateur Swimming
Association (CASA) Master Official from Pointe Claire, Quebec, became its Canadian representative and
then regional manager, running Omega swimming sales, rental and service across the country.[^sn36][^sn38] A newsletter of August 1978 called his
first year in the Montreal area a success.[^sn46]

The last Seagull advertisement found is from January 1979.[^sw7901] By November 1979 an Omega advertisement
directed American buyers to "Our U.S. Office", at the address of John F. Bickel, P.E., of Hatboro,
Pennsylvania, who also appears in it as a sales agent.[^sw7911] [Sportyme](sportyme.md) was listed at the
same address from 1980. No source found gives the reason for the change, says whether Seagull ended
the agency or lost it, or records what became of the company.

## Products

This section lists the lines Seagull sold, other than through its Omega agency. The American Aquatics
Division distributed [Cronus](cronus.md) digital stopwatches, and in 1976 Seagull called itself the only
factory-authorized Cronus distributor in swimming.[^sw7603][^sw7606] In March 1976 it offered Cronus
watches and Omega equipment together as low-cost alternatives, from six stopwatches in a case at $400.[^sw7603]

In 1977 the range widened. Seagull added [Heuer](heuer.md) stopwatches in May, and in June it announced
exclusive distribution of the [Sycom](sycom.md) Pasar pacing system and [Pacedyne](../equipment/common/pace-clock/pacedyne.md)
battery pace clock, along with the [Microsel](microsel.md) Racer wrist chronograph.[^sw7705][^sw7706] Its
advertising moved to the line "Seagull is the source" and a list of dealers.[^sw7707] In late 1978 it began
selling [Accusplit](accusplit.md) memory stopwatches directly, and by December it had a toll-free
number.[^sw7811][^sw7812]

Seagull stopped distributing Cronus in Canada by August 1978, leaving that trade to its dealer
[Mod International](mod-international.md), and said it remained a major Cronus distributor in the United
States.[^sn46]

## In swim timing

This section covers Seagull's Omega business. Its first advertisements offered the Swim-O-Matic with
touchpads adapted to hang in American gutters, for purchase or for rent at a stated minimum of $750 a
day.[^sw7305] It demonstrated the lower-priced OSM-4 at the 1973 Canada Games in New Westminster, British
Columbia, where by its own account the organizers bought the unit.[^sw7309] Six-lane and eight-lane
touchpad systems were priced at $8,500 and $9,600 in November 1973.[^sw7311] The OSM-5 followed in October
1975 at a starting price of $5,500, or $7,700 in Canada.[^sw7510][^sn18]

Seagull advertised directly against [Colorado Time Systems](colorado-time-systems.md) (CTS) in 1976, in a
full-page table comparing the OSM-5 with the CTS console.[^sw7610] The table is Seagull's, and it dated the
CTS details to a coaches' clinic packet of May 1976. It priced six-lane and eight-lane systems at $5,525 and
$6,825 for Omega against $5,614 and $6,655 for CTS, and contrasted Omega's perforated touchpads and 12 V battery operation with the CTS sealed touchpad and mains
power. Elsewhere it promoted the [Omega touchpad](../equipment/swimming/touchpad/ocp5.md) as the part that
decides a system's reliability, and cited tests run by Don Watson, an OSM-5 owner.[^sw7311][^sw7710]

The company offered a trade-up program in 1974, and a 1976 page of customer
statements stressed its support.[^sw7410][^sw7608] By August 1978 it listed service points in Montreal,
Toronto, Edmonton and Vancouver as well as California and Pennsylvania, with
[Spectronics](spectronics.md) of Edmonton as the newest contractor.[^sn46] The same newsletter said it had
chosen [Daktronics](daktronics.md) to supply low-cost scoreboards that would work with Omega timing
systems, and that a Daktronics board had gone into the natatorium at Brantford, Ontario.[^sn46] It counted a
new system for the Crystal Pool in Victoria as the 28th Omega system it had put into a Canadian pool.[^sn46]

## In competition

This section records events and sites that Seagull named or that the press connected with it. Its October
1974 advertisement listed pools and meets that had chosen Omega that year, among them the NCAA Championships
at Belmont Plaza, the AAU Championships at Concord, the Canadian Nationals at Ottawa and the Canada Games Pool.
The list also included the 1974 European Championships in Vienna and the 1976 Olympic Games in Montreal.[^sw7410] That year it also said CASA had
endorsed and recommended Omega systems, and a 1975 Swim Canada article named Seagull among the
sponsors supporting Canadian swimming.[^sw7410][^sn17]

Seagull staff attended the 1976 Olympic Games in Montreal, and the company invited customers to meet them
there.[^sw7607] Gibbons had assisted at the Olympic pool, and Swim News described Seagull as timer of the last
three Canada Games.[^sn38] In 1977 Swimming World reported that Seagull would install donated Omega timing equipment, intended for studying body motion, at the Squaw Valley Olympic Training Center.[^sw7709]

The Omega equipment at the 1978 Commonwealth Games in Edmonton was sold by Seagull, which offered tours of
its installations there and hosted a suite for customers.[^sn46] That autumn its advertising used the line "The Timers of The Olympics ... Commonwealth Games and The Pan Am Games", and in December it called itself a supplier to the Olympics.[^sw7809][^sw7812]

In August 1978 Seagull also announced a large role at Lake Placid: it expected to provide much of the timing and scoreboard equipment for the 1980 Winter Olympics alongside Swiss Timing, and to resell some of the boards at a discount afterward.[^sn46] No other source found confirms that this happened.
